newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Luz del Sur sale draws $76 mln in 1st week.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Luz del Sur sale draws $76 mln in 1st week.

text.p: The Peruvian government said Monday national individuals offered to buy shares in Luz del Sur worth 196 million soles ($76 million) in the first week of its sale of a 30 percent stake in the electricity distributor.

"We are very satisfied with the demand in the first stage of the share placement," said government privatization official, Jhonny Kadena, on announcing initial results of the sale that began last Monday.

Hoping to raise -- at home and abroad -- a total of $200 million from the sale, privatization officials have said they expect Peruvian individuals to buy between 55 percent and 60 percent of the government's stake.
The government expects institutional investors at home and abroad to buy the remainder of its stake in the share placement, with the price to be set on December 10.
The government will define the distribution of the shares it sells on December 13.
Officials from investment bank CS First Boston -- chosen by the government to handle the international portion of the sale -- expect the placement abroad to raise about $100 million.
The domestic portion of the sale will be divided into two parts.
In the sale of shares to individual Peruvian nationals, Banco Continental will direct a group of local banks that includes Banco de Credito, Interbanc and Banco Wiese.

In the second part of the local sale, Spain's Banco Santander has been selected to handle the placement with local institutions. The Spanish bank's brokerage in Peru, Santander SAB, will direct a group of local brokerages to book build with institutions such as local pension funds, insurance companies and banks.

In June 1994, a consortium consisting of Chile's Chilquinta International Inc and Canada's Ontario Hydro bought a 60 percent stake in Luz del Sur, a former state-run electricity company, for $212.1 million.
Another 10 percent stake is owned by the company's workers.

In July, there was so much unsatisfied local demand after the placement of state-held shares in Telefonica del Peru that the government was forced to sell a further three percent stake in the company after the original offer closed.
In the end, the Telefonica sale of a total 26.6 percent stake brought the government $1.25 billion.
